title: The observer that changed the answer
subtitle: Discovering that my own profiler caused the serialisation it reported, and retracting a verdict I had already acted on

stats.label: copy and compute overlap with timing-enabled events on, from 0.02
overlap with no events, or with release-build events only, up to 1.09
variants interleaved in one process to test the instrument

lede: A trace from my instrumented runtime showed that host-to-device copies were not overlapping with compute on the Intel card. I believed it, and I made a design decision on it. Then a controlled experiment showed that the timing events I had enabled to see the overlap were themselves the reason there was none. I retracted the verdict in the plan, and every overlap claim since gets an uninstrumented variant before anyone acts on it. Whether copies and compute overlap on a GPU decides the whole economics of a memory layer that stages data across the bus every step. You cannot see overlap without instrumentation, and instrumentation touches the thing it measures.
evidence: GPU profiling and instrumentation: showed timing-enabled events serialised host-to-device copies behind compute, overlap 0.02-0.21 with them against 0.79-1.09 without.
Performance experiment design: 3 instrumentation variants interleaved in one process, so the card, the driver and the host load were identical for all of them.
Intel GPU and SYCL/oneAPI engineering: traced timing events to timestamp commands on the compute engine that made the copy engine wait, on the Level Zero runtime.
Scientific integrity in engineering: a written retraction of my own verdict in the plan, and a standing rule that every overlap claim gets an uninstrumented control.
author: Corey James
